epidemiology.title: New brief highlights gaps and recommendations for improving violence data on women - World Health Organization (WHO)
epidemiology.summary: A new technical brief calls for more consistent and rigorous measurement of non-partner sexual violence against women and girls – a widespread form of violence that remains underreported and inadequately measured.Non-partner sexual violence, defined as sexual violence perpetrated by someone other than an intimate partner – is a global public health and human rights issue with serious consequences for women’s physical, mental, sexual and reproductive health. An estimated 263 million women and girls aged 15 years and older, or 8% globally, have been subjected to sexual violence from a man other than an intimate partner at least once since the age of 15 years. The prevalence is likely to be much higher because of gaps in available evidence, measurement challenges and the underreporting associated with stigma and fear of repercussions.The new brief by the UNDP/UNFPA/UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP), the World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations partners, identifies key measurement challenges and provides recommendations to researchers, statistical offices and others designing population-based surveys for strengthening the measurement of non-partner sexual violence.Where are the gaps?WHO’s review of population-based surveys, conducted between 2000 and 2023, identified 140 countries with at least one eligible survey, covering 89% of the global population of women and girls aged 15 years and older.

epidemiology.title: Translating evidence to action: One year of postpartum haemorrhage guideline implementation - World Health Organization (WHO)
epidemiology.summary: In 2026, postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) remains a leading cause of maternal mortality globally, underscoring the urgent need for sustained action across all levels of healthcare systems. One year after the publication and landmark launch of the WHO-FIGO-ICM Consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of PPH at the XXV FIGO World Congress in Cape Town, this World PPH Day webinar will convene global experts to reflect on progress, share implementation experiences and accelerate action to reduce the burden of PPH worldwide.Led by FIGO in collaboration with HRP (the UNDP/UNFPA/UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction), the World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), this session will examine how countries, professional societies, healthcare providers and partners are translating evidence into practice. Speakers will provide updates on progress against the Roadmap to Combat Postpartum Haemorrhage between 2023 and 2030, highlight the new implementation guide published earlier this year and share lessons learned from implementing the guidelines across diverse health system contexts.Drawing on the perspectives of leaders from international organisations, the frontlines of obstetrics and midwifery, and national ministries of health, presentations will showcase real-world implementation experiences and outcomes, spotlighting successes, challenges and transferable strategies for improving PPH prevention, diagnosis and treatment.Following an audience Q&A, this webinar will conclude with a renewed call to action for FIGO's member societies and partners to advocate for the review and adaptation of the guidelines at the national level, support the implementation and uptake of updated PPH guidance, strengthen healthcare workforce capabilities and foster collaboration across disciplines and sectors to drive collective action in the fight against PPH.Register for the webinar today and join the global movement translating evidence into action to end preventable maternal deaths from PPH: https://figo.ooo/46bOut1.

The findings support mind-body therapies as potentially useful supportive care—but they did not substantially reduce pain intensity, an important distinction between feeling less pain and functioning better despite it.
